requirements: The core contributions of DistServe — disaggregating prefill and decoding computation onto separate GPU instances with per-phase parallelism/placement optimization to maximize per-GPU goodput under TTFT/TPOT SLOs — have been reproduced.

sub_tasks.requirements: The hardware cluster (4 nodes × 8 A100-80GB with NVLINK intra-node, 25Gbps cross-node), CUDA/NCCL stack, Ray runtime, and required Python/C++ dependencies to run DistServe are available.
The physical/virtual GPU cluster matches the paper's testbed of 4 nodes × 8 A100-80GB GPUs with NVLINK intra-node and 25 Gbps cross-node bandwidth (Section 6.1).
Code has been implemented (e.g., a `scripts/check_cluster.sh` or Python probe) that queries `nvidia-smi -L` and asserts each node exposes 8 NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB devices with 80GB of HBM per GPU.

Code has been implemented that runs `nvidia-smi topo -m` (or `nvidia-smi nvlink --status`) and verifies intra-node GPU pairs report NVLINK (NV*) connectivity rather than PCIe/SYS, matching the paper's NVLINK-equipped nodes used by the low node-affinity placement.
Code has been implemented (e.g., a small `iperf3` / NCCL bandwidth probe wrapper) that measures point-to-point cross-node bandwidth between two cluster nodes.

The measured cross-node bandwidth reported by the probe is approximately 25 Gbps (consistent with the paper's stated cross-node bandwidth in Section 6.1), and the probe fails/warns if bandwidth deviates by more than a documented tolerance.
The cluster launcher / hostfile enumerates 4 reachable nodes with SSH/Ray connectivity, and a startup script asserts a total of 32 GPUs are visible across the cluster before any experiment starts.
The CUDA toolkit and NCCL library required by DistServe's C++/CUDA parallel execution engine and by the orchestration layer's cross-node KV cache transfers are installed and functional.

A CUDA toolkit (nvcc) with a version compatible with A100 (SM 8.0) is installed, and the environment setup script asserts `nvcc --version` succeeds and PyTorch reports `torch.cuda.is_available() == True` with `torch.version.cuda` populated.

NCCL is installed and discoverable (via `libnccl.so` on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` or PyTorch's bundled NCCL), and a probe runs `torch.distributed.init_process_group(backend='nccl')` across at least two GPUs and completes an `all_reduce` without error.

Code has been implemented that launches a NCCL send/recv between GPUs on two different nodes (exercising the 25 Gbps cross-node path used for KV cache transfer) and asserts the transfer completes end-to-end, validating the cross-node NCCL setup DistServe relies on.
A Ray runtime is installed and can form a multi-node cluster so DistServe can spawn its per-instance Ray actor GPU workers (Section 5).

Ray is installed at a version compatible with the DistServe engine, and `python -c 'import ray; ray.init(); print(ray.cluster_resources())'` succeeds on the head node, exposing `GPU` in the cluster resources dictionary.

A cluster startup script (`ray start --head` on the head node and `ray start --address=...` on worker nodes) is provided, and after startup `ray.cluster_resources()` reports GPU count = 32 aggregated across the 4 nodes.
The Python and C++/CUDA build/runtime dependencies needed to compile DistServe's ~8.1K LOC C++/CUDA engine and run its ~6.5K LOC Python orchestration are installed and reproducible.

A `requirements.txt` / `pyproject.toml` (or environment YAML) pins the Python dependencies needed by the orchestration layer and frontend — including PyTorch (with CUDA), Ray, transformers/tokenizers, FastAPI/uvicorn (for the OpenAI-compatible REST API), numpy, and pyyaml — and `pip install -r requirements.txt` completes without unresolved conflicts.

A C++/CUDA build toolchain (g++ ≥ 9, CMake ≥ 3.18, ninja, and CUDA headers) is installed, and running the engine's build script (e.g., `pip install -e .` or `bash build.sh`) successfully compiles the C++/CUDA extension modules (continuous batching kernels, PagedAttention, FlashAttention bindings) without errors on an A100 host.

A smoke test script loads the compiled engine, allocates a small FP16 tensor on an A100 GPU, runs a single forward pass through a toy transformer block, and asserts the output is finite — confirming the full CUDA+PyTorch+engine stack is functional end-to-end before any DistServe experiment is launched.

The C++/CUDA parallel execution engine — supporting continuous batching, PagedAttention, FlashAttention, MHA/GQA-capable transformer inference, intra-op (tensor) and inter-op (pipeline) parallelism, and Ray-actor GPU workers with distributed KV cache management — is implemented and runs correctly for OPT.
The engine's build system, C++/CUDA source tree, and Python bindings are structured as described in Section 5 (~8.1K lines of C++/CUDA).
Code has been implemented that provides a C++/CUDA source directory (e.g., csrc/ or engine/) with CMakeLists / setup.py building a Python-importable extension exposing engine entry points.

Code has been implemented that exposes a Python-facing engine class (e.g., ParallelExecutionEngine / Worker) with methods for load_model, forward_prefill, forward_decode, and KV-cache allocation, backed by the compiled C++/CUDA extension.
Code has been implemented that builds successfully against CUDA and produces a smoke-test executable/pytest that instantiates the engine on 1 GPU and runs a single forward pass without errors.
OPT transformer inference (MHA, learned absolute positional embeddings, FP16) is implemented so that OPT-13B/66B/175B checkpoints load and produce correct logits/next-token distributions.
Code has been implemented for an OPTDecoderLayer (multi-head self-attention with MHA, FFN with ReLU, LayerNorm, residual connections) matching the OPT architecture used in the paper.
Code has been implemented that uses OPT's learned absolute positional embeddings with a max supported sequence length of 2048 tokens (matching the paper's LongBench truncation rationale).

Code has been implemented that loads HuggingFace OPT-13B/66B/175B FP16 weights into the engine's own tensor layout (with sharding when TP>1) and verifies parameter counts against the checkpoint metadata.
A unit test verifies that the engine's forward pass on OPT-13B for a fixed prompt reproduces the HuggingFace reference next-token top-1 id (greedy) and top-5 logit ordering.

Code has been implemented with a GQA-capable attention code path (num_kv_heads configurable independently of num_query_heads) so newer models with GQA/MQA can be run through the same kernels (Section 6.1).
FlashAttention and PagedAttention kernels are integrated so that prefill uses FlashAttention over contiguous KV tensors and decoding uses PagedAttention over block-based KV storage.
Code has been implemented that invokes a FlashAttention CUDA kernel (Dao et al. 2022) for the prefill phase attention computation.
Code has been implemented for a PagedAttention CUDA kernel (Kwon et al. 2023) that reads K/V from a paged block table and computes attention for decoding steps.
A unit test verifies FlashAttention and PagedAttention produce numerically equivalent outputs (max abs diff < 1e-2 in FP16) to a naive PyTorch attention reference on the same Q/K/V.
Code has been implemented that appends the new K/V rows produced during a decoding step into the paged KV cache blocks in the correct block/offset positions.
The engine manages a distributed, block-based KV cache across GPU workers with allocation, free, and cross-worker addressing.
Code has been implemented for a BlockManager that maintains a free-block pool per GPU, allocates blocks per request/sequence, and releases them on completion.
Code has been implemented that shards KV cache across TP-workers by head dimension and across PP-workers by layer dimension consistently with the model's weight sharding.
A unit test verifies the block table for a sequence of length L uses ceil(L/block_size) blocks and that freeing the sequence returns them to the free pool.

A measured test confirms that the total KV cache size for a single 512-token OPT-66B request is approximately 1.13 GB (as stated in Section 3.3), computed from the engine's per-block byte size × allocated blocks.
Continuous (iteration-level) batching is implemented so that new requests can join a running batch and finished sequences leave without a full-batch restart (Yu et al. 2022).
Code has been implemented for an iteration-level scheduler that assembles a batch of (prefill-token OR one-decode-token)-per-sequence for each forward step.
Code has been implemented that supports mid-batch admission of newly arrived requests and mid-batch eviction of sequences that emitted EOS or reached max tokens, without restarting the batch.

A unit test drives 4 requests with staggered arrival into a single engine and asserts that (a) each produces the same output as running it standalone and (b) the engine performs fewer forward-passes than sequential execution.
Intra-operator (tensor) parallelism is implemented for OPT with NCCL all-reduce collectives on QKV, attention output, and FFN layers.

Code has been implemented that column-parallel shards QKV projections and FFN gate/up layers and row-parallel shards attention output and FFN down layers, with NCCL AllReduce on the row-parallel outputs.

Code has been implemented that allows TP degrees of at least {1, 2, 3, 4, 8} to be configured per instance (matching the placements reported in Table 3, including the TP=3 prefill instance for OPT-175B).
A unit test with TP=2 on a single node verifies that the sharded forward pass produces logits equal (within FP16 tolerance 1e-2) to the TP=1 forward pass on the same prompt.
Inter-operator (pipeline) parallelism is implemented so OPT layers are partitioned into PP stages with inter-stage activation communication and microbatching.
Code has been implemented that partitions the OPT layer stack into PP contiguous stages, one stage per worker group, and passes hidden activations between adjacent stages via point-to-point sends.
Code has been implemented that runs pipeline microbatches concurrently so that at steady state all PP stages are busy on different microbatches (1F1B-style schedule).
A unit test with PP=2 verifies that the pipelined forward pass produces the same next-token id as PP=1 on the same prompt for OPT-13B.
Ray-actor GPU workers implement the distributed runtime, launching one actor per GPU and coordinating parallel execution.
Code has been implemented that defines a Ray @ray.remote GPU Worker actor class with methods for init_model, load_weights, execute_step, and get_kv_cache_info.
Code has been implemented that initializes a NCCL communicator group across the Ray actors for a given TP×PP topology and stores rank/world_size on each actor.
A unit test brings up Ray with 2 GPU actors (TP=2) on a single node, executes a forward pass through the actor RPC path, and asserts non-null token output on the driver.
Measured engine performance reproduces the paper's per-phase compute characterization for OPT-13B on a single A100 (Figure 3, §3.1–3.2).

A measured benchmark reproduces Figure 3(a): prefill throughput for OPT-13B on 1×A100 saturates around a 512-token single sequence, with the input=512 curve reaching the plateau within the paper's tolerance.

A measured benchmark reproduces Figure 3(b): decoding throughput for OPT-13B on 1×A100 rises monotonically with batch size across {1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128} for input lengths {128,256,512,1024}, matching the paper's shape.

A measured benchmark reproduces the prefill-decoding interference in Figure 2: adding a single prefill job of input length 128 (and 1024) to a decoding-only batch slows both prefill and decoding as batch size scales, matching the trend in the paper.

A measured benchmark reproduces Figure 5: for OPT-13B decoding with batch size 128 and input length 256, intra-op parallelism reduces latency with diminishing returns while inter-op parallelism scales throughput near-linearly across {1,2,4,8} GPUs.

The DistServe orchestration layer that creates independent prefill and decoding instances, transfers KV caches across instances (NCCL cross-node, asynchronous CudaMemcpy intra-node), and exposes an OpenAI-compatible REST frontend is implemented per Figure 6.
The overall runtime architecture from Figure 6 (Controller + independent Prefill and Decoding Instances) is implemented, with each instance holding its own copy of the model weights.
Code has been implemented that exposes a runtime module with distinct classes/objects for Controller, PrefillInstance, and DecodingInstance matching the components shown in Figure 6.

Each PrefillInstance and DecodingInstance loads and manages exactly one complete copy of the LLM weights (spanning multiple GPUs when model parallelism is applied), verifiable by a unit test that instantiates each type and inspects the weight state.

PrefillInstance and DecodingInstance can be independently instantiated (different counts, different parallelism configs) without either depending on the presence of the other in the same process/GPU set.

Prefill and decoding instances register themselves with the central Controller on startup so the Controller maintains a queryable directory of live instances and their (inter-op, intra-op) configuration.

The centralized Controller receives all incoming requests and performs two-stage dispatch (to shortest-queue prefill instance, then to least-loaded decoding instance) as described in Section 4.3 and shown in Figure 6.
Code has been implemented for a Controller class whose public API accepts an incoming request object (prompt + sampling params) and returns/streams the generated response.

Given multiple prefill instances with different queue depths, the Controller dispatches a new request to the prefill instance with the shortest pending queue (verifiable via a unit test that stubs instance queue lengths).

After a prefill instance completes the first token for a request, the Controller dispatches the request to the least-loaded decoding instance (verifiable via a unit test that stubs decoding-instance loads).

The Controller tracks per-request lifecycle state (arrived, prefill-dispatched, prefill-done, kv-transferred, decoding-dispatched, decoded, returned) so metrics/latency-breakdown queries can attribute time to each stage.

The Controller supports many-to-one prefill-to-decoding mapping (e.g., multiple prefill instances routing into a single decoding instance) as described in Section 2.3 and used by the placement algorithm outputs.

The KV cache transmission subsystem transfers intermediate state between prefill and decoding instances using NCCL for cross-node and asynchronous CudaMemcpy for intra-node paths, and implements the pull-based, layer-aligned scheme from Section 4.3 and Section 5.
Code has been implemented for a KV-cache transfer manager module that both prefill and decoding instances plug into for handing off per-request KV tensors.

The transfer manager initializes NCCL communicators between corresponding prefill and decoding GPU workers whenever the two instances are placed on different nodes, and uses NCCL send/recv (or equivalent collective) for the KV payload.
When prefill and decoding workers share a node, the transfer manager routes KV cache via asynchronous CudaMemcpy (e.g., cudaMemcpyAsync on a dedicated non-default stream) instead of NCCL.

The KV transfer path is non-blocking with respect to GPU compute: a unit/integration test launches a transfer concurrently with a matmul on the source GPU and confirms the matmul does not stall waiting on the copy.

The transfer uses a pull model — the decoding instance initiates the KV fetch from the prefill instance when it is ready to start decoding, not a push from prefill on completion (verifiable by inspecting the control flow / mocking sender vs. receiver).

The prefill instance retains completed-request KV cache blocks in its GPU memory as a queuing buffer until the decoding instance pulls them, and frees them only after a pull acknowledgment (buffer-lifetime test).

The KV transfer is layer/stage-aligned: for inter-op-parallel instances, KV blocks for a given transformer layer are exchanged only between the prefill and decoding worker(s) holding that same layer stage (per Section 4.2 low-affinity design).
For OPT-66B in FP16 with MHA, the measured (or analytically computed) KV cache size for a single 512-token request equals approximately 1.13 GB as reported in Section 3.3.

A bandwidth-requirement helper (or documented derivation) reproduces the paper's calculation that a 10 rps stream of 512-token OPT-66B requests demands ≈ 90 Gbps of KV cache transfer bandwidth to render the overhead invisible.
The RESTful frontend exposes an OpenAI-compatible interface accepting sampling parameters (max output length, temperature) and streaming generation back, as described in Section 5.
Code has been implemented for an HTTP server (e.g., FastAPI/uvicorn) that exposes an OpenAI-compatible completions endpoint (e.g., /v1/completions) accepting JSON with a `prompt` field.

The frontend honors a `max_tokens` (maximum output length) sampling parameter and enforces it at the decoding instance (verifiable by a unit test that requests N tokens and asserts the returned completion length ≤ N).
The frontend honors a `temperature` sampling parameter (temperature=0 yields deterministic greedy output; temperature>0 propagates into the sampler used by the decoding instance).
The frontend supports streamed responses (e.g., server-sent events / chunked HTTP) so tokens are delivered as decoding produces them, matching the OpenAI streaming schema.
The frontend routes each incoming HTTP request through the central Controller and returns the decoding instance's final text back to the client in the OpenAI response schema.
Distributed GPU worker management uses Ray actors, per Section 5, so each instance's parallel workers can be launched, addressed, and coordinated by the orchestration layer.

Code has been implemented that spawns each instance's per-GPU workers as Ray actors (importing `ray` and using `@ray.remote` / `ActorHandle`) and stores the actor handles inside the PrefillInstance/DecodingInstance objects.
The Ray-actor workers each own and manage their shard of the KV cache in a distributed manner (no single central KV store), so KV blocks live where their layer/tensor shard is computed.

Instance-level workers are launched according to the (inter-op, intra-op) parallelism configuration emitted by the placement algorithm (e.g., an OPT-175B ShareGPT run instantiates prefill workers with TP=3, PP=3 and decoding workers with TP=4, PP=3 as reported in Appendix B Table 3).
End-to-end integration and implementation-scale properties of the orchestration layer match what the paper reports in Section 5.

An integration test drives one request end-to-end (HTTP frontend → Controller → PrefillInstance → KV transfer → DecodingInstance → streamed response) using a small stub model and asserts the client receives generated tokens.

The combined Python implementation of the placement-algorithm module, RESTful frontend, and orchestration layer totals approximately 6.5K lines of Python code, matching the count reported in Section 5.

The event-driven simulator that predicts prefill/decoding execution time from FLOPs and memory accesses (Appendix A latency model) and reports SLO attainment given workload traces is implemented and its accuracy vs. real system is within the paper's reported error.
The analytical latency model (Appendix A) that estimates per-step execution time from FLOPs and memory accesses is implemented.

Code has been implemented that computes prefill-phase FLOPs as a function of model hyperparameters (hidden size, number of layers, number of heads, vocab size) and the batch's total input token count, matching the transformer prefill FLOP formula used in Appendix A.

Code has been implemented that computes decoding-phase FLOPs as a function of model hyperparameters, current batch size, and per-request context length (KV cache length) used for the incremental attention step.
Code has been implemented that computes the memory-access volume (weights + KV cache reads/writes) per prefill and per decoding step so the memory-bound branch of the latency model can be evaluated.

Code has been implemented that turns FLOPs and memory-access counts into a predicted step latency using device peak FLOPS, HBM bandwidth, and a calibrated efficiency factor, as described in Appendix A.
Code has been implemented that profiles a small set of reference prefill/decoding kernels on the target GPU once and stores the resulting efficiency/roofline constants for reuse by the latency model.

The latency model, when evaluated on isolated prefill and decoding steps at representative batch sizes and sequence lengths, predicts per-step latency within the accuracy tolerance implied by the paper's simulator error (well under 10% mean absolute error against measured kernel times).
The event-driven simulator core that plays back a workload trace over prefill and decoding instances is implemented.

Code has been implemented that provides an event queue advancing simulated wall-clock time through discrete events (request arrival, batch start, batch finish, KV transfer complete) in chronological order.

Code has been implemented that ingests a workload trace of (arrival_time, input_length, output_length) tuples — either from a real dataset or resampled from a fitted distribution — as the simulator's request source.

Code has been implemented that fits input/output length distributions from a historical trace and can resample new traces from that distribution, matching the paper's description of the simulator's workload input.

Code has been implemented providing a `simu_prefill(config, workload)` entry point that simulates a prefill instance with the given parallelism configuration and returns per-request TTFT and achieved goodput, as called by Algorithms 1 and 2.

Code has been implemented providing a `simu_decode(config, workload)` entry point that simulates a decoding instance with the given parallelism configuration and returns per-request TPOT and achieved goodput.
Code has been implemented that models FCFS request queuing at each instance, so waiting-time contributions to TTFT/TPOT match the M/D/1-style behaviour analyzed in Section 3.1.
Code has been implemented that models continuous batching for the decoding instance, growing/shrinking the running batch as new decode-eligible requests arrive and existing ones finish.

Code has been implemented that models inter-op (pipeline) parallelism as sequential per-stage execution with the appropriate number of in-flight microbatches, including the pipeline bubbles caused by variable prefill lengths described in Section 3.3.

Code has been implemented that models intra-op parallelism by applying a configurable speedup coefficient K (1 < K < 2 for 2-way, generalized for higher degrees) to per-step execution time, matching the analysis in Section 3.1.

Code has been implemented that models the KV-cache transfer between prefill and decoding instances by computing per-request KV-cache size and dividing by the configured inter/intra-node bandwidth to add a transfer delay event.
The simulator returns identical per-request TTFT/TPOT results across repeated runs on the same seeded trace and configuration (deterministic replay).
The simulator reports SLO-attainment metrics that downstream placement algorithms and evaluations consume.

Code has been implemented that, given the simulated per-request TTFT and TPOT traces and configured TTFT/TPOT SLOs, computes the fraction of requests meeting both SLOs (SLO attainment) reported by Table 2.
Code has been implemented that binary-searches over request rate to find the maximum rate at which a target SLO-attainment goal (e.g., 90%) is achieved, as used by Algorithms 1 and 2.

SLO attainment reported by the simulator monotonically decreases (non-increasing) as request rate increases for both vLLM-style colocated and DistServe-Low configurations, matching the trend in Table 2.
The simulator's SLO-attainment predictions match the real system within the accuracy the paper reports in Table 2.

Across all rates and both configurations reported in Table 2 (vLLM and DistServe-Low, rates 1.0–4.0 req/s), the maximum absolute error between simulator-reported and real-system SLO attainment is less than 2 percentage points, matching the paper's claim that error is <2% in all cases.

For the vLLM (colocated) configuration at rate = 1.0 req/s on the ShareGPT-style workload, the simulator reports SLO attainment matching the real system to within 2 percentage points of Table 2's 97.0% (real) vs 96.8% (simulator) row.

For the vLLM (colocated) configuration at rate = 2.0 req/s, the simulator reports SLO attainment matching the real system to within 2 percentage points of Table 2's 52.8% (real) vs 51.0% (simulator) row.

For the vLLM (colocated) configuration at rate = 4.0 req/s, the simulator reports SLO attainment matching the real system to within 2 percentage points of Table 2's 23.6% (real) vs 24.1% (simulator) row.

For the DistServe-Low configuration at rate = 2.5 req/s, the simulator reports SLO attainment matching the real system to within 2 percentage points of Table 2's 87.3% (real) vs 88.3% (simulator) row.

For the DistServe-Low configuration at rate = 4.0 req/s, the simulator reports SLO attainment matching the real system to within 2 percentage points of Table 2's 70.0% (real) vs 68.9% (simulator) row.

Algorithm 1 — enumerating per-phase parallel configurations, calling simu_prefill/simu_decode with binary search for max goodput, and replicating to meet target rate — is implemented and produces the expected placements for the tested models.
The Algorithm 1 procedure and its I/O contract are structurally implemented as described in Section 4.1.

Code has been implemented that exposes a high-node-affinity placement function (e.g., `high_node_affinity_placement`) taking the paper's Algorithm 1 inputs — LLM G, per-instance node limit N, GPUs-per-node M, GPU memory capacity C, workload W, and target traffic rate R — and returning a `best_plm` placement object.

Code has been implemented so that the returned placement carries the prefill parallel configuration (inter-op, intra-op), the decoding parallel configuration (inter-op, intra-op), and the number of replicas needed to meet R.

Code has been implemented that operates without cross-node colocation constraints — any (prefill instance, decoding instance) pair may be placed on any two nodes of the cluster, matching the high-affinity assumption of Section 4.1.
Enumeration of feasible per-phase parallel configurations subject to cluster and memory constraints.
Code has been implemented that enumerates all (inter_op, intra_op) parallel configurations for the prefill instance whose total GPU count is at most N·M.
Code has been implemented that enumerates all (inter_op, intra_op) parallel configurations for the decoding instance whose total GPU count is at most N·M.
Code has been implemented that discards any enumerated configuration whose per-GPU model shard (weights plus expected KV cache working set) exceeds the GPU memory capacity C.

Code has been implemented that fits an arrival/length distribution from a historical workload W and resamples traces to feed the simulator, per Section 4.1's discussion of workload prediction over long timescales.
Per-configuration binary search over rate using simu_prefill / simu_decode to find the maximum goodput meeting the SLO attainment target.
Code has been implemented that, for each enumerated prefill configuration, invokes `simu_prefill(config, resampled_trace)` and returns per-request TTFT results usable to compute SLO attainment.
Code has been implemented that, for each enumerated decoding configuration, invokes `simu_decode(config, resampled_trace)` and returns per-request TPOT results usable to compute SLO attainment.

Code has been implemented that runs a binary search over the arrival rate for a fixed configuration, returning the maximum rate at which the simulator reports SLO attainment >= the user-specified target (e.g., 90%).

The binary search behaves monotonically: increasing the queried rate never increases the reported SLO attainment for a fixed configuration, and the search terminates within a bounded number of simulator calls.

Code has been implemented that selects the prefill config and the decoding config with the highest per-GPU goodput independently (i.e., without coupling their parallel-strategy searches), as prescribed by the two-level algorithm in Section 4.1.
Replication to match the user-required overall traffic rate and assembly of the final placement.
Code has been implemented that replicates the chosen prefill and decoding instances by counts derived from their per-instance goodputs so that the aggregated served rate is >= R.

Code has been implemented so that the number of prefill replicas per decoding replica may exceed 1 when decoding goodput per instance exceeds prefill goodput per instance, matching the paper's observation that multiple prefill instances can be allocated per decoding instance.
Numerical/behavioral claims about Algorithm 1 from Section 4.1 and Section 6.5.
The implemented Algorithm 1 wall-clock running time scales approximately as O(N·M^2) as the per-instance GPU count (N·M) grows, consistent with the complexity claim in Section 4.1.

The implemented Algorithm 1 completes end-to-end placement search in under 1.3 minutes on the paper's largest reported setting (32 GPUs per instance) when run on a multi-core CPU host, matching Section 4.1's claim.
